During my time using the iPhone 18 Pro, I also conducted a small experiment, since the iPhone Duo is about to launch and everyone is eagerly looking forward to it.

In order to get a preview of the large-screen user experience of the upcoming new device, I used an iPad mini as a phone replacement for a period of time. Because the screen size and shape are similar, I hoped this would roughly simulate the actual operating experience...

I'll admit first that buying an iPad mini was a bit of an extravagance. Most of the time it was used only as an e-reader, borrowing library books through the Libby app—because in the UK, you can't read those books on a Kindle. (Don't get me started on this strange shortcoming...)

Given the number of e-books I read, buying an extra device largely dedicated to reading isn't entirely unreasonable, but I do feel a bit guilty that such a capable piece of hardware is only serving such a limited function. However, I've now at least found a temporary new task for it: getting an early feel for what using the iPhone Duo might be like.

As my colleague Ryan Christoffel mentioned earlier, the iPhone Duo's internal screen is slightly smaller than the iPad mini's, but the difference isn't... all that big.

Since the iPhone Duo has much thinner bezels, the gap in screen size isn't as noticeable as you might think: iPhone Duo: 7.6-inch screen; iPad mini: 8.3-inch screen.

My approach was to install all the apps I have on my iPhone, keep the layout as consistent as possible, and get as close to the real experience as I could. The iPhone's Wi-Fi hotspot feature provided the connectivity I needed, allowing me to use the iPad in situations where I'd otherwise be using my phone.

In some ways, the iPad mini experience is better than the Duo's, because it runs iPadOS rather than iOS, which offers more flexible multitasking. However, I don't really enjoy using windowed mode on a screen this small, so I mostly use apps in full-screen or split-screen mode, which makes the interface very similar to that of the Duo.

To deal with the fact that it doesn't fit in a pocket, I only took it out when I was carrying a backpack, and I carry a backpack for roughly half the time I'm out and about.

Of course, the iPad doesn't support every feature of the Duo, so this is only a very rough simulation of the experience, but it did give me a general sense of what it's like to own a phone with a screen this size—and I thoroughly enjoyed the process.

Many similar comparisons tell us that the biggest落差 often doesn't come when you switch to the new product, but at the moment you switch back to the old one. Every time I switched from the iPad mini back to the iPhone 18 Pro, the screen felt astonishingly small. This experiment has done nothing to dampen my anticipation for the new device.
